title: Pituitary Gland & Sella Turcica Atlas
subtitle: Explore pituitary compartments, sellar relationships and hypothalamic control
altText: Chalkboard-style midsagittal and coronal views of the pituitary gland within the sella turcica, labelled with the optic chiasm, cavernous sinuses, sphenoid sinus, hypothalamus and infundibulum.
learningObjectives: Locate the pituitary gland within the sella turcica and identify its relationships to the optic chiasm, cavernous sinuses and sphenoid sinus.
Differentiate anterior and posterior pituitary organisation, inputs and outputs.
Relate sellar expansion and pituitary dysfunction to plausible visual, endocrine, neurological and psychological presentations without over-localising symptoms.

sections.explainSimply: The pituitary is a pea-sized hormone gland in a bony pocket beneath the brain. It receives instructions from the hypothalamus and helps regulate growth, stress, reproduction, thyroid function, water balance and lactation.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: The pituitary is a major endocrine interface between brain and body. Changes in pituitary or hypothalamic function can alter energy, sleep, mood, cognition, sexual function, appetite and stress physiology, but these symptoms are nonspecific and require medical assessment.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: The hypophysis sits in the hypophyseal fossa of the sphenoid bone. The anterior lobe receives hypothalamic releasing and inhibiting factors through the superior hypophyseal portal circulation; the posterior lobe contains axon terminals from supraoptic and paraventricular hypothalamic neurons. Superiorly lie the diaphragma sellae, infundibulum and optic chiasm; laterally are the cavernous sinuses containing the internal carotid arteries and cranial nerves III, IV, V1, V2 and VI; inferiorly lies the sphenoid sinus. Sellar and parasellar lesions may therefore combine endocrine, visual-field, ocular-motor, facial sensory and headache presentations.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Think of the hypothalamus as the executive office and the pituitary as the dispatch centre. The sella is the reinforced control booth, but nearby visual and cranial-nerve cables make expansion clinically important.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Pituitary disease can mimic or amplify depression, anxiety, fatigue, cognitive slowing, irritability, sleep disturbance and changes in motivation. Psychologists should recognise red flags and avoid assuming that endocrine-linked symptoms are purely psychological.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Pituitary hormone excess or deficiency can produce broad systemic and neuropsychiatric effects. Expanding masses may compress the optic chiasm, invade the cavernous sinus or disturb hypothalamic pathways. Symptom patterns vary with hormone type, lesion size, growth direction, treatment and comorbidity.
sections.clinicalPearl: A combination of new visual-field change, persistent headache and endocrine symptoms is a sellar-region red flag, not a personality formulation.
sections.clinicalExample: A person with fatigue, reduced libido, headaches and difficulty noticing objects at the outer edges of vision may require urgent medical and visual-field assessment for a sellar or suprasellar process; no single symptom proves pituitary disease.
sections.limitationsCautions: Hormonal symptoms are often gradual and nonspecific. Imaging size does not map neatly onto symptom severity, incidental pituitary lesions are common, and psychiatric presentations should not be attributed to pituitary dysfunction without endocrine and medical evidence.
sections.practicalExample: Use the relationship view to predict whether a lesion expanding superiorly, laterally or inferiorly would be more likely to affect vision, cavernous-sinus structures or the sphenoid sinus.

anatomy.position: Midline in the hypophyseal fossa of the sphenoid bone, inferior to the hypothalamus and optic chiasm, between the cavernous sinuses and superior to the sphenoid sinus.
spatialRelationships: Optic chiasm usually superior and slightly anterior
inputs: Hypothalamic releasing and inhibiting hormones via portal vessels
Magnocellular axons from supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei
outputs: Vasopressin and oxytocin released from posterior pituitary terminals
connections: Posterior pituitary water-balance and reproductive pathways
bloodSupply: Superior hypophyseal arteries, usually from internal carotid and posterior communicating branches
Inferior hypophyseal arteries from cavernous internal carotid branches
Portal venous plexus linking median eminence to anterior pituitary
lesionPatterns: Bitemporal visual-field loss from chiasmal compression
Ocular-motor or trigeminal symptoms with cavernous-sinus extension
Diabetes insipidus with stalk or posterior-system involvement
Nonspecific fatigue, mood or cognitive change requiring endocrine correlation
associatedPresentations: Changes in growth, weight or body composition

stages.label: Hypothalamus
stages.text: Hypothalamic neurons detect internal state and generate releasing, inhibiting or neurosecretory signals.

stages.label: Pituitary route
stages.text: Signals travel through portal blood to the anterior lobe or down axons to the posterior lobe.

stages.label: Target organs
stages.text: Pituitary hormones influence thyroid, adrenal, gonadal, growth, lactation and water-balance systems.

stages.label: Feedback
stages.text: Peripheral hormones and physiological state feed back to hypothalamic and pituitary systems.

explorerParts.label: Anterior pituitary
explorerParts.detail: The adenohypophysis synthesises and releases ACTH, TSH, GH, prolactin, LH and FSH under hypothalamic and peripheral feedback control.
explorerParts.clinical: Functional adenomas may produce hormone excess; compression or treatment can reduce multiple axes.

explorerParts.label: Posterior pituitary
explorerParts.detail: The neurohypophysis stores and releases vasopressin and oxytocin made in hypothalamic magnocellular neurons.
explorerParts.clinical: Stalk or posterior-system injury can disturb water balance; diabetes insipidus is not expected from most isolated anterior adenomas.

explorerParts.label: Optic chiasm
explorerParts.detail: Crossing nasal retinal fibres lie close to the superior sellar region, although exact chiasmal position varies.
explorerParts.clinical: Superior expansion can cause classically bitemporal field loss, but visual patterns depend on anatomy and compression geometry.

explorerParts.label: Cavernous sinuses
explorerParts.detail: Each cavernous sinus contains the internal carotid artery and is related to cranial nerves III, IV, V1, V2 and VI.
explorerParts.clinical: Lateral extension may cause diplopia, ophthalmoplegia or facial sensory symptoms; these require urgent medical evaluation.

explorerParts.label: Sphenoid sinus
explorerParts.detail: The sphenoid sinus lies inferior to the sellar floor and provides the common transsphenoidal surgical route.
explorerParts.clinical: Its anatomy matters for surgery and explains why inferior relationships differ from superior chiasmal effects.

quiz.question: Which structure is most vulnerable to a pituitary mass expanding superiorly?
quiz.rationale: The optic chiasm lies immediately superior to the sella, so superior expansion can disturb crossing visual fibres.

quiz.question: How does the hypothalamus primarily control the anterior pituitary?
options: Through releasing and inhibiting hormones carried in portal vessels
quiz.rationale: Hypothalamic factors enter the hypophyseal portal circulation at the median eminence and regulate anterior pituitary cells.

quiz.question: Which statement is clinically safest?
options: Mood and fatigue symptoms are nonspecific and require endocrine and medical correlation
Pituitary lesion size predicts psychiatric severity exactly
A normal mood excludes pituitary disease
quiz.rationale: Neuropsychiatric symptoms can occur in endocrine illness but are nonspecific and should not be used as stand-alone localisation evidence.
